# phig rules — by invariant

## conflict

### R01 — holds

A protected destination is never overwritten under any on_conflict policy; the resolver renames around it.

The protected set covers another image's not-yet-moved source and any real file the database does not track. Overwriting either destroys bytes phig cannot restore, so the guard outranks the policy the user asked for.

| | |
|---|---|
| Enforced at | `core/paths.cpp:resolve_conflict` |
| Binds | `organize.copy`, `organize.move`, `organize.plan` |
| Protects | original-file |
| Evidence | witness: `OrganizeEngineTest.OverwritePolicyStillRenamesAroundAnExistingFile` |

### R02 — holds

A move to an occupied destination fails rather than replacing what is there, whatever the conflict policy decided.

This guard sits below the planner and answers a question the plan cannot: a file that appeared at the destination after planning, from a concurrent phig run or a sync app. It uses the kernel's atomic no-replace rename where one exists, then a hard-link emulation, so the check and the rename are one operation rather than two.

| Enforced at | `core/paths.cpp:move_file`, `core/paths.cpp:rename_noreplace` |
| Binds | `organize.move`, `remove.trash` |
| Protects | original-file, attachment |
| Evidence | witness: `MoveFileTest.RefusesToOverwriteExistingDest`, `MoveFileTest.CrossDeviceRefusesToOverwriteExistingDest`, `OrganizeExecTest.MoveRefusesAnOccupiedDestinationWithoutAuthorization`, `RemoveExecTest.TrashTwoSameNameFilesGetDistinctPathsNoClobberAndLogs` |

### R03 — holds

A destination already claimed by an earlier file in the same run is a conflict even when nothing occupies it on disk.

Two selected files can expand to one destination under the same format string. The first has not been written yet when the second is resolved, so no on-disk check can see the collision; only the claimed set can.

### R05 — holds

The copy branch renames an occupied destination aside before writing and puts it back if any step fails.

Defense in depth: the planner protects every existing on-disk path, so in normal use the destination is free, and this covers any caller that targets an occupied one anyway. The backup is a same-directory rename rather than a byte copy, so every failure path can restore it, and a failed restore is thrown rather than swallowed because the original then sits only at the backup path.

| | |

| Enforced at | `core/organize_exec.cpp:execute_organize_action`, `core/paths.cpp:unique_backup_path` |
| Binds | `organize.copy` |
| Protects | original-file |
| Evidence | witness: `OrganizeExecTest.CopyRestoresPriorFileOnDbFailureOverwrite`, `OrganizeExecTest.CopyOverwriteSuccessLeavesNoBackup` |

### R06 — holds

An authorized replace renames the occupant aside before the move and restores it if any later step fails.

move_file refuses to overwrite, so an occupied destination has to be cleared before the rename can succeed; doing it with a same-directory rename means the disk action, the path update and the log entry can all be undone. The backup is removed only after the transaction commits, which is the point at which the replacement the caller authorized has actually happened.

### R08 — violated (test gap)

A run started with on_conflict overwrite replaces the file at an occupied destination.

The flag offers three values and the code has two behaviors. The planner's is_protected returns true for any path that exists on disk and resolve_conflict renames around a protected destination, so a run-level overwrite differs from rename only on an intra-run collision. A user who asks to replace a file gets a renamed copy instead and is not told. R01 records the guard that produces this and is correct on its own terms; what is wrong is that the policy name promises something the guard never allows.

### R09 — holds

An explicit per-item override may replace a file that exists on disk, but never another image's not-yet-moved source.

An override is the caller answering a conflict the plan showed, which is the opposite of the silent loss the on-disk arm of the guard exists to stop, so that arm is bypassed. A batch source is a tracked original phig is in the middle of relocating; no caller intent makes destroying it correct, so an override that lands on one is refused rather than honored.

### R10 — holds

A destination that became occupied between plan and apply is skipped, never re-resolved to a name the caller was not shown.

Re-running the resolver at execution time could file the photo under a name that appeared in no plan, which defeats the point of authorizing one. Skipping keeps the outcome a subset of what was shown, and the item lands in the skipped count so the caller can re-plan and see the new conflict. An item carrying an explicit override is exempt, because that override is the authority to replace what is there.

| | |
|---|---|
| Enforced at | `core/organize_engine.cpp:OrganizeEngine::apply` |
| Binds | `organize.copy`, `organize.move` |
| Protects | original-file |
| Evidence | witness: `OrganizeEngineTest.ApplySkipsAnItemWhoseDestinationBecameOccupied`, `OrganizeEngineTest.ADestinationThatBecameFreeIsSimplyWritten` |

### R11 — holds

A file whose resolved destination is its own path is left alone: nothing is written and nothing is logged, a resolution only the overwrite policy produces.

resolve_conflict's occupancy test has no self-exemption, so a file already sitting at its destination reads as taken and never takes the free-path branch. Only the overwrite arm then returns the path unchanged, because the is_protected predicates do exempt a file's own source; under rename the resolver falls into the suffix loop and files the photo beside itself under a _1 name, and under skip it returns empty. On the path that does reach the executor the guard is what stops a move renaming a file onto itself and logging a meaningless entry, and stops the copy branch running its backup-then-copy dance against the very file it is copying.

| | |

| Enforced at | `core/organize_exec.cpp:execute_organize_action` |
| Binds | `organize.copy`, `organize.move` |
| Protects | original-file, activity-log |
| Evidence | witness: `OrganizeExecTest.NoOpSelfMoveDoesNothingAndLogsNothing`, `OrganizeExecTest.NoOpSelfCopyDoesNotCorruptFile`, `ResolveConflictTest.SelfSourceNotProtected` |

### R69 — holds (test gap)

Writing a command's results to the path named by --output does not destroy what is already at that path.

Results are rendered into a buffer and written through write_output_file, which creates a temporary sibling with O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW and renames it into place, so the path never holds a partial file and a symlink planted at the temp's name is never written through. The parent directory must exist: none is created. The rename refuses an occupied path, a symlink included (dangling or not), unless --overwrite was given; with it the rename replaces the link itself and never the file it points at. cmd_duplicates and all three branches of cmd_search (person, face, general) go through one ResultSink, and fav list reaches cmd_search, so no site opens the path itself. --count with --output and --overwrite without --output are refused before any work is done, as flags that would do nothing. cmd_search and cmd_duplicates also refuse an occupied path before the search runs, to save the work; the refusal in write_output_file is the one that holds. Every other write phig makes refuses an occupied destination (R01, R02, R41), and this one now does too. Libphig returns records and leaves the writing to its caller, so the write and its guard live in core/paths.cpp for any surface that renders results to a file.

### R81 — holds (test gap)

Staging a stdin query image does not destroy anything already on disk.

search --similar - and search --face - read stdin into memory first, so empty stdin is refused before anything is created. The bytes are then written through write_private_temp_file, which creates the file with mkstemp in fs::temp_directory_path(): a unique name, O_EXCL, mode 0600. No existing path or symlink is opened, so nothing already on disk is truncated or written through, and concurrent stdin searches get different files. The CLI removes the staged file when the search ends, on every path including a thrown exception, through a destructor in cmd_search.

## reconcile

### R12 — holds

A tracked path is deletable only when its file is gone and its parent directory still exists; a missing parent and a failed existence check are reported apart from it and kept.

A missing file alone does not say what happened. A missing parent directory usually means an unmounted or unreachable subtree rather than a deletion, and an existence check that errors says nothing at all. The three cases warrant different treatment, so the classifier returns them separately and leaves the judgement to the caller instead of collapsing them into one filtered list.

| Binds | `scan.reconcile`, `remove.orphans` |

A path whose existence could not be determined is never deleted, under any flag.

### R15 — holds (test gap)

Scan skips its whole destructive phase when every tracked row under the scanned directory classifies as deletable.

An unmounted drive is indistinguishable from a deleted collection at the point reconcile runs, and losing a whole subtree's tags and faces to a forgotten mount is worse than leaving stale rows behind. The guard compares the deletable set against every row under the prefix, so it fires only when the two are the same size. A run that also has rows in parent_missing or check_failed does not trip it, and its deletable rows are deleted: those other rows are held by the per-row classifier of R12, not by this guard. The guard is coarse on purpose, and it names the flag that overrides it.

### R16 — holds

A stale row's user metadata transfers only when exactly one other tracked file with the same sha256 exists on disk; with none or several it transfers nowhere and the row is still deleted.

With two identical-content files on disk phig cannot tell which one the user moved, and guessing would attach the tags to the wrong photo. The cost of refusing is real and is recorded rather than hidden: the row is deleted either way, and the restore snapshot captures neither tags nor faces, so ambiguity destroys them. Choosing a target is a feature nobody has designed, not an override of this rule.

### R75 — holds (test gap)

Which rows a scan deletes is decided by whether their files are on disk, never by which files that scan's flags admitted to the walk.

run_reconcile takes its candidate set from db_.get_paths_with_prefix(scan_prefix) — every tracked row under the scanned directory — and classifies it with paths_safe_to_delete, which asks the filesystem. --recursive, --media and --hidden filter the walk instead (core/scan_engine.cpp:131-146) and reach none of that, so narrowing a scan cannot turn a row into a deletion candidate. That is worth stating because the opposite is the natural reading of the flags: a scan told to look at images only, in one directory only, still leaves every video and every subdirectory row alone. Measured with the built binary against a three-file collection (an image, a video, and an image in a subdirectory) scanned recursively: a following non-recursive `--media image` scan of the same directory reported Removed: 0 and left all three rows. The converse holds too, because the candidate set is the prefix rather than the walk — with the subdirectory's image then deleted from disk, a non-recursive `--media video` scan of the same directory reported Removed: 1 and dropped that row, a file the walk neither entered the directory for nor would have admitted. The prefix is where the containment argument sits: scanning a subdirectory reconciles that subtree and nothing above it.

## atomicity

### R28 — holds

Every write transaction opens with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so a transaction that reads and then writes cannot fail with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT.

SQLite in WAL mode pins a read snapshot at the first read of a deferred transaction; if another connection commits before this one writes, the upgrade fails with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT, which the busy handler does not retry — so the 30-second busy_timeout does not help and the write simply fails. Taking the write lock at BEGIN turns that failure into a wait. Every read-then-write path in the engine has this shape: delete_paths_logged reads a row to snapshot it before deleting it, log_prune scans operations before deleting them, and init_schema reads the version before writing it.

| Binds | `scan.walk`, `scan.reconcile`, `organize.copy`, `organize.move`, `remove.trash`, `remove.hard`, `remove.db-only`, `remove.orphans`, `relink.transfer`, `relink.demote`, `relink.demote_live_photo`, `metadata.write`, `faces.rebuild`, `faces.identify` |
| Protects | db-row, user-metadata, activity-log |

### R29 — holds (test gap)

Each schema migration takes the write lock before it reads the version and re-reads the version inside that transaction, so a step another process already applied is skipped rather than re-run.

The migrations are not idempotent — ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN fails the second time — so two first runs starting together would otherwise both apply the same step and one would die. Re-reading inside the IMMEDIATE transaction means the loser sees the winner's version and moves on. The two schema-creation paths have the same shape for the same reason: each creates every table and sets the version in one transaction, so a crash partway cannot leave a versionless partial schema that the next run misreads as pre-migration.

| Protects | db-row, user-metadata, activity-log |
| Evidence | witness: `DatabaseConcurrency.ConcurrentMigrationIsSafe`, `DatabaseConcurrency.AMigrationStepAnotherThreadAppliedIsSkippedInsideTheTransaction`, `SchemaUpgradeTest.APreMigrationRepairAnotherConnectionOvertookIsSkipped`, `SchemaUpgradeTest.AFreshSchemaOvertakenByANewerBuildIsRefusedAndNotRestamped` |

Measured with the re-check deleted from init_schema, it failed 0 of 20 runs. AMigrationStepAnotherThreadAppliedIsSkippedInsideTheTransaction forces what that one hopes for: a third connection holds the write lock while both threads read version 4 and then block on the first migration's BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so one applies every step and the other finds them applied from inside its own transaction. Each thread's init_schema is timed, because a thread that had read the current version would have returned without opening a transaction at all — that is the assertion which says the window was entered. With the same re-check deleted it failed 20 of 20. What is still uncovered is the two schema-creation paths' one-transaction shape, which neither test reaches. The pre-migration path re-reads the version inside its IMMEDIATE transaction too, and commits nothing when another connection has created or upgraded the schema since its first read; without that it would stamp a current schema v1 and fail its v2 step for good. APreMigrationRepairAnotherConnectionOvertookIsSkipped forces that interleave: a pre-migration database, a second connection holding the write lock until the first has written its pre-upgrade copy, then a current version committed in its place. With the re-read removed it failed 3 of 3, the database left at v1 and the open failing on the v2 step. The fresh-schema path re-reads as well. Its statements are CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS or INSERT OR IGNORE, but set_schema_version is INSERT OR REPLACE, so without the re-read it would stamp a newer build's schema back down to this build's version. AFreshSchemaOvertakenByANewerBuildIsRefusedAndNotRestamped holds the write lock while the opening connection waits on that path's BEGIN IMMEDIATE, then commits a newer version in its place; with the fresh path's re-read disabled it fails, the open succeeding against the newer schema. |

### R30 — holds (test gap)

Reconcile's relink and demote passes commit one row at a time and its deletes commit as a single transaction, so an interruption between them leaves the copied fields on both rows — tags always, gallery when the target had none — the transferred faces on the target alone, and every stale row still present.

The two halves have different failure costs. A transfer copies two of its three fields and moves the third: transfer_user_metadata unions tags onto the target and fills an empty gallery, leaving both in place on the source, while its faces clause is UPDATE faces SET image_id = ?, a move that strips the source row when it fires (R37). So a per-row commit that stops halfway leaves the copied fields duplicated and the faces on the target only, and neither state costs a label — the next scan re-derives the duplication and then deletes the stale row, and the moved faces already sit on the row that pass designated as the survivor. The deletes are the destructive half and go in one transaction, so a stopped run has dropped every stale row or none of them. The ordering between the passes is load-bearing and is pinned: relink runs before demote, so a shared target takes the moved row's gallery rather than the demoted JPEG's.

### R31 — holds (test gap)

log_begin_operation commits its operation row on its own before the first entry, so an interrupted run leaves an operation behind — marked interrupted by rm and by reconcile when the failure is an exception, and left in_progress when the process dies.

Opening the operation outside the work's transaction is what makes the row survive a rollback: delete_paths_logged rolls back its own transaction on failure and the operation row stays, so the run is not invisible. The cost is that the terminal status is a second write. Only two of the three callers close the loop: cmd_rm and run_reconcile catch, mark the operation interrupted on a best-effort basis and rethrow, while OrganizeEngine::apply catches per file and writes interrupted when any file or attachment failed (R27). A process that dies instead — a signal, a crash, the machine going away — leaves in_progress under every caller; plan 020 recorded that when it wrote log_finish_operation, noting the state is harmless for its own slice and meaningful for the deferred viewer that still does not exist.

### R32 — holds

OrganizeEngine::apply moves or copies one media file, then commits that file's path update and log entry in a single transaction and compensates if it fails, before starting the next — so a run that stops partway leaves every media file before the stop point moved and recorded and every one after it untouched.

A rename cannot go inside a SQL transaction, so the disk action happens first and outside: move_file runs, then begin_transaction covers only update_path_in_txn and log_add_entry. What makes the pair behave as a unit is compensation rather than a shared transaction — a database failure moves the file back, and a failed move-back is thrown with both paths named rather than swallowed, because the file then sits somewhere no row names. The unit is the media file alone: carry_sidecars runs after execute_organize_action has returned and its transaction has committed, so an attachment moved for that file is outside this boundary and is R33's window, not this rule's.

### R33 — holds (test gap)

A change that touches only the disk — trashing a file, hard-deleting it, carrying a sidecar or an attached JPEG — is written to disk first and logged afterwards in its own autocommit, so an interruption between the two leaves the change done and unrecorded.

A rename and a SQLite commit cannot be one transaction, so one of them goes first, and these paths put the disk action first. Nothing compensates for the gap: execute_organize_action moves a file back when its database write fails, and execute_trash_action and carry_sidecars have no equivalent — if log_add_entry throws, the file stays where it was put and the log does not mention it. carry_sidecars catches that failure per attachment, counts the file in carried and also lists it in failures, so the caller learns of the missing log entry through attachment_errors. For trash that means a file sitting in the trash directory under a random-hex name with nothing recording where it came from, which is the one case where the name alone does not say.

### R34 — unenforced (test gap)

A committed transaction survives a process crash but not necessarily an operating-system crash or a power loss: the connection runs WAL with synchronous=NORMAL, which does not fsync the write-ahead log at every commit.

This is the durability the pragma buys and the cost it accepts, and no plan states either. The consequence is bounded rather than arbitrary: move_file and atomic_copy_file fsync the file and its parent directory before the rename, so the bytes are on disk even when the row naming them is not, and the state a power loss can leave — the file at the destination, the row still naming the source — is the one execute_organize_action's compensation already handles and a rescan reconciles. Recorded because a reader who sees BEGIN IMMEDIATE everywhere will otherwise assume commits are durable against everything.

A copy or move counts each selected item once: an item is reported as applied or as failed, never as both.

### R62 — partial (test gap)

No C++ exception crosses an ABI entry point.

Where a phig_ctx* is in scope the body is wrapped in PHIG_TRY/PHIG_CATCH, which converts an exception into a status plus a thread-local message: LockBusy to PHIG_ERR_BUSY, any other std::exception to PHIG_ERR_DB, anything else to PHIG_ERR_INTERNAL. PHIG_TRY expands to a null check on ctx, so the ctx-less entry points cannot use it and wrap their bodies in a plain try/catch(...) instead — phig_init does, and so do twelve of settings.cpp's thirteen. The exception is phig_settings_free, a bare { delete s; } with no handler, counted below among the 39. The hole is the entry points that return something other than phig_status. Scripted over phig.h's 69 PHIG_API declarations, 39 have no handler of their own. Most are trivially non-throwing accessors, or delegate to a wrapped helper — phig_op_copy_start and phig_op_move_start both call start_apply, which uses PHIG_TRY. But phig_query_add_tag push_backs a std::string, the ten phig_query_set_* functions assign one, and phig_op_poll copies the path and error strings, so each can throw std::bad_alloc into a C caller with no way to catch it. No plan states this.

### R64 — holds (test gap)

Adding a symbol bumps PHIG_ABI_VERSION_MINOR and the CMake VERSION, and never SOVERSION.

SOVERSION is the major alone, so an additive, backward-compatible change keeps the soname and existing callers need no rebuild; only an incompatible change bumps SOVERSION and MAJOR. The two numbers are hand-maintained in two files and agree today — phig.h has MAJOR 1 and MINOR 3, libphig/CMakeLists.txt has VERSION 1.3.0 and SOVERSION 1, with a comment there saying it must track the header. CI compares them on every push: scripts/rules.py's check_abi_version reads MAJOR and MINOR out of the header and VERSION and SOVERSION out of the CMake file and fails when the three disagree, which phig_abi_version() cannot do — it packs the two header macros together, so a test comparing it to the header cannot see that either has drifted from the CMake value. What no check reaches is the trigger. Adding a symbol needs no edit to the export lists, which match on the phig_ prefix rather than on a list of names, so a new entry point ships exported with both numbers untouched and every comparison still agreeing. The version bump is the only manual step and therefore the only one that can be forgotten.

Measured by adding a PHIG_API void phig_break_the_pin(void); to the header: '70 exported symbols and ABI 1.3 was recorded with 69'. What stays open is that a count is not a set. phig_op_progress gains no field: a new counter means a new struct and a new poll symbol.

The struct is caller-allocated and filled by phig_op_poll, with no size and no version member, so a client built against an older header would have a newer libphig.so write past the end of its buffer — corruption the client cannot detect, not an error it can check for. phig_op_progress2 with phig_op_poll2 is the additive answer and keeps the soname. ### R80 — violated (test gap)

A scan whose indexing phase failed does not run its reconcile phase, so nothing is deleted on the strength of a walk that did not finish.

Reconcile deletes rows whose files it could not find, so running it after a walk that aborted partway would delete rows for files that were simply never reached. --on-error fail is the flag that makes that reachable: an unreadable file makes run_workers flush what completed and rethrow, and cmd_scan catches the exception, prints it and returns 1 at cli/main.cpp:324-334, above the run_reconcile call at :340. ScanEngine::run composes the two the same way, run_workers then run_reconcile with a throw from the first propagating past the second (core/scan_engine.cpp:110-114), but it has no production caller — cli/ and libphig/ both call the split phases — so the sequencing has to be re-stated by every caller, and that is why this is recorded as violated rather than as a property of the engine. Cancellation is the other side of the same decision and goes the other way deliberately: an interrupted walk returns completed = false rather than throwing, and cmd_scan reconciles anyway, which is safe for the same reason the statement is needed — a file the walk never reached is still on disk, so it is not a deletion candidate (R75) — and R56 records that reconcile polls no token once it starts.

### R88 — holds (test gap)

A schema migration step fails only on foreign key violations it creates, and no step runs until a backup of the database has been written.

Steps run with foreign keys off (R84), so apply_migration_step reads PRAGMA foreign_key_check inside the step's transaction before and after the step, and rolls back only if the after set holds a violation the before set does not. A violation is identified by child table, child rowid and parent table, not by the foreign key's index, which a table rebuild can renumber. Because the identity is the rowid, a future step that rebuilds a table without an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, such as image_tags, renumbers its rows and makes every orphan in it read as new, so the step would fail; such a step must carry the rowids across (INSERT ... SELECT rowid, ...). Checking the whole database instead failed every step on rows no step had made: a catalog carrying faces rows whose images row was deleted before foreign keys were enforced could not reach any later version, and since reads refuse an outdated catalog (R70) and every write opens through an upgrade, no version of phig could open it for writing. Existing orphans are carried through unchanged; deleting them would make an upgrade destroy rows, labels among them, on its own authority, and whether to repair them is a separate destructive decision this rule does not make. Upgrades are automatic and forward-only and a catalog newer than the build is refused, so an upgrade cannot be undone by running the older phig. write_upgrade_backup therefore writes VACUUM INTO a new file beside the database, named for the version read and the UTC second (phig.db.v7-backup-20261113T201500Z), and flushes the file to disk, and its directory on a best-effort basis, before the first step's transaction — VACUUM INTO cannot run inside one — and before the pre-migration path's schema repair. The name is claimed with an exclusive create, so an existing file is never overwritten; a name already taken, as by a second process upgrading in the same second, gets a numeric suffix. If the copy cannot be written or the file cannot be flushed, init_schema throws before any step and the database is unchanged. settle_upgrade_backup keeps the copy, reports it through upgrade_backup_path and logs it at warning level only when this connection committed a step. When it committed none — the upgrade failed before its first commit, or another process applied every step first — the database is not what the copy guards against losing, so the copy is removed; otherwise every retried open of a catalog that cannot upgrade would leave another one. A process that loses a concurrent upgrade partway keeps its copy, which may hold a later version than its name says, but no process runs a step before its own copy is on disk. phig never deletes a copy that a committed step depends on. Measured on a synthetic catalog of 30,000 images with one face and embedding each: the copy took about 50 ms on tmpfs and 70-76 ms on ext4/NVMe within a 340-424 ms upgrade from v7.

### R04 — partial (test gap)

Deleting a row captures a restore snapshot sufficient to rebuild that row's user-authored metadata.

A rescan rebuilds hash, EXIF and thumbnails. It cannot rebuild a tag someone typed, a gallery assignment, or a face label. ### R18 — holds (test gap)

A log entry describing a database change is inserted inside the same transaction as that change, so the log never records a change that did not commit.

The log is the only account of what an operation did, and an account that disagrees with the database is worse than none, because a future undo would restore against a state that never existed. Every writer has the same shape: open a transaction, make the change, add the entry, commit — so a rollback takes the entry with it. delete_paths_logged widens the idea to a batch, with one BEGIN IMMEDIATE covering every row it deletes and every purge_row entry it writes.

### R19 — holds

No entry in the activity log is ever updated or deleted on its own; the only removal is log_prune, which drops whole operations oldest-first and always keeps the newest.

A trail that can be edited in place records what someone wanted to have happened. The only statements against operation_entries are one INSERT in log_add_entry and the cascade from log_prune's DELETE FROM operations WHERE id <= ?, so an entry can only leave with the operation it belongs to; the cascade depends on PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON, set on every open. Keeping the newest operation even when it alone exceeds the cap is what stops a run pruning away its own record.

The default removal mode moves a file into phig's trash directory under a generated name, retrying with a fresh one if that name is taken, so the removal is reversible from disk and never destroys what is already in the trash.

Trash is what lets rm be the ordinary removal command: the row goes, the bytes stay. The trash name is the file's stem plus eight random hex characters, generated rather than searched for, so there is no window between choosing a name and taking it. Uniqueness is not asserted: move_file refuses to clobber and throws errc::file_exists, and execute_trash_action loops back for a fresh name — that retry, not the randomness, is what makes the no-clobber claim true. ### R27 — holds (test gap)

An operation that did not do everything it was asked to do is recorded with a terminal status that says so.

cmd_rm counts its per-file failures and writes interrupted when there were any. OrganizeEngine::apply checks a destination with the non-throwing exists, so a destination it cannot inspect counts as an error rather than escaping and leaving the operation in_progress. It derives completed from three facts, not cancelled, no parent that failed (errors) and no attachment left behind (attachment_errors), and writes interrupted exactly when completed is false, so the same fact, some files did not make it, gives the same terminal status whichever command wrote the log. cancelled is reported separately, so a caller can tell a stopped run from one that failed. cmd_organize returns 1 whenever completed is false, as cmd_rm does, and phig_organize_result carries both flags while the operation itself ends PHIG_OP_DONE unless cancelled. Plan 053 is about what a client can reach through the ABI, not about what an operation destroys or how it counts, so it did not own this; plan 060 did.

### R83 — holds (test gap)

An operation that fails against the database reports the cause: the message it raises names what SQLite refused, not the state of the connection after the rollback that followed.

Each of the three delete-path sites in core/database.cpp (delete_paths, delete_paths_logged, log_prune) reads sqlite3_errmsg into the message before any rollback, so the text names what SQLite refused. sqlite3_errmsg reports the connection's most recent result, and a successful ROLLBACK would overwrite it with 'not an error'. Any throw inside the transaction, including delete_faces_for_image and log_add_entry, is caught, rolled back once through rollback_if_open and rethrown unchanged. rollback_if_open runs ROLLBACK only when the connection is not in autocommit and swallows any error, so it cannot replace the exception being thrown and cannot leave the transaction open under the caller's terminal status write. The message is what cmd_rm's and run_reconcile's callers print and what the diagnostic log records; the activity log has no reason field (R27), so this text is the only account of the failure. The shape matches step_write_or_throw and the migration blocks, which already rethrow with their text intact.

## metadata

### R35 — holds

A re-scan of an already-indexed path updates that row in place rather than replacing it, so the row keeps its id and the tags, favorite and gallery attached to it.

INSERT OR REPLACE deletes the row before inserting the new one, and with foreign_keys=ON that cascades image_tags and faces away and hands the file a new id, so every re-scan would silently strip the one thing a re-scan cannot rebuild. ON CONFLICT(path) DO UPDATE keeps the id and rewrites only the derived columns — hash, phash, dimensions, metadata blob, effective date — and gallery is not in the SET list at all, so a re-scan cannot clear it. The favorite flag needs no clause of its own because it is a row in image_tags like any other tag. Plan 022 finding #1 made this change. Measured with the built binary: tagging a file, favoriting it, setting its gallery and then re-scanning with --force left the tag, the favorite, the gallery and the row id exactly as they were.

### R36 — holds (test gap)

A re-scan of a file whose sha256 differs from the one recorded, or with none recorded, clears the row's unnamed faces and keeps its named ones until a re-detection carries their labels or reports them dropped; when the two match it keeps every face — boxes, embeddings and person labels.

A face box and its embedding describe pixels, so once the bytes change they describe pixels that no longer exist; an unnamed face holds nothing else and goes. A named face also holds a person label, which is user-authored and which nothing can reconstruct, so it stays: Database::insert keeps it with its box, embedding and model, and marks its frame replaced (frame_source 'replaced', frame hash and size unknown), which also keeps carry_labels from matching it by box overlap against a frame it was never measured in. A RAW's faces are measured on its sidecar JPEG or embedded preview, never on the file, so the mark has to be explicit; comparing a face's frame hash with the row's would call every RAW face replaced. A scan that detects faces then hands the image to replace_faces, the routine face rebuild uses, on both its changed-file and unchanged-file paths: carried labels are written onto the new detections, an unmatched one is dropped and counted in ScanResult::labels_dropped, and the CLI warns. A scan that detects no faces, such as libphig's index, leaves the named faces kept for the next face rebuild or face-detecting scan. An unchanged file must not lose a label to an ordinary re-scan, and --force hash alone must not either: the test is the hash, not the flag.

### R37 — holds

A metadata transfer unions the source's tags onto the target, fills the target's gallery only when it has none, and moves the source's faces onto it only when the target has none; the source's tags and gallery are left in place.

The three fields fail differently, so they are resolved differently. Tags are a set and a union loses nothing, and the favorite flag rides along because it is a tag. A gallery is a single value, so one of the two has to win, and the target's is the later statement of intent — the user assigned it to the row that still has a file. Faces are the same choice with a sharper edge: detections already on the target came from the pixels that are still there, so stale boxes must not displace them, and the count is checked in C++ rather than as a NOT EXISTS in the UPDATE, which would see the rows it had just moved and stop after one. Faces are also the one field that leaves the source changed. The clause is UPDATE faces SET image_id = ?, a move rather than a copy, so a transfer that fires strips the source row of its faces — DatabaseTest.TransferUserMetadataMovesTagsGalleryFaces asserts exactly that. Each caller commits its own transfer alone, and the source row is deleted afterwards in a separate transaction that run_reconcile opens once every pass has finished, so a source row stripped of its faces and not yet deleted is a state the database really passes through and an interrupted run can leave standing; R38 is the ordering and R30 is the rule that owns what an interruption in that window leaves behind. The window costs no label: the faces sit on the row the pass designates as the survivor, and the next scan finishes the deletion. Measured by forcing the window by hand — moving a labelled face to the target and leaving the source row in place — then re-scanning, which removed the source row and left the face and the name alice on the target. The statement names what is left in place because a caller that transferred between two rows it meant to keep would find the source stripped, and no other rule would tell it.

### R39 — holds

When a moved row and a demoted JPEG both transfer into the same surviving row, the moved row's gallery is the one that lands, because relink runs before demote and a gallery transfer fills only an empty target.

The case is ordinary: a RAW moves on disk and a JPEG sits beside its new location, so relink_moved_rows and demote_jpeg_rows both target the RAW's row. A person label is typed by a user and cannot be derived again from pixels, while a rebuild replaces every face row of the images it selects. FacesEngine::run reads the image's labelled faces inside the per-image transaction before deleting them, carry_labels matches them to the new detections, greedy and one-to-one, and the matched labels are written before auto_label_face names the rest. Matching is by embedding when the recognition model is unchanged and by intersection over union at kLabelCarryMinOverlap when the model changed and the recorded frame is identical to the new decode (R86). Labels with no match are counted in FacesResult::labels_dropped.

### R86 — holds (test gap)

Under an unchanged recognition model a carried face label lands only on a re-detected face whose unit-normalized embedding lies within kLabelCarryMaxDistance of the labelled face's; after a model change it lands only on a face overlapping at kLabelCarryMinOverlap within a frame recorded as identical (same bytes by sha256 and same size); any other label is dropped and counted, and a label never moves by box position across frames that are not recorded identical.

kLabelCarryMaxDistance is 1.128, SFace's published same-identity threshold on unit-normalized embeddings. A rebuild re-detects faces and carries each image's labels onto the new detections. Box positions depend on the decoded frame, which can change without changing its size — a square image rotated 90 degrees, any image rotated 180 degrees or mirrored — so a box match can attach a name to the wrong person with no signal. carry_labels therefore matches by embedding when the recognition model is unchanged, since embeddings come from aligned face crops and do not depend on the frame, and by box overlap only when the model changed and the face rows record a frame identical to the new decode (same bytes by sha256, same size). Anything else is dropped and counted in labels_dropped. A wrong label is worse than a dropped one: a drop is reported, a wrong label is not. The two passes share one set of taken detections, so a detection takes at most one label across both. FacesEngine records a file's row sha256 as the frame hash only while the file's mtime and size still match the row; otherwise the frame hash is empty and the overlap pass cannot match. A same-model embedding match is a biometric threshold, not an identity: a lookalike within it, such as a relative when the labelled person is cropped out or not re-detected, can take the label.

## attachments

### R41 — holds

A carried attachment never overwrites an occupied destination, on copy as well as on move.

move_file declines and throws, but atomic_copy_file ends in a rename that replaces silently. An attachment has no row, so a destroyed one leaves no restore snapshot and no error — the run reports Errors: 0. A refused carry is reported in CarryResult::failures and counted in attachment_errors. An attachment's destination is derived from its parent's rather than chosen, and the conflict planner never sees it, so there is no skip/overwrite/rename policy to consult and nothing renames it aside: refusing is the only available answer. The guard sits at all three carry sites — metadata sidecars, a Live Photo's video, a RAW's attached JPEG — because they end in the same two primitives. Measured with the built binary: a cp whose planned destination directory already held the parent's .xmp left that file's contents intact and reported the failure.

## concurrency

### R07 — holds (test gap)

A read-then-write on a face row labels only the face it compared: an id whose face was deleted in the gap is out of circulation and matches nothing, and `person_id IS NULL` refuses a face another labeler named first.

The face subcommands and libphig's faces operation both run lock-free, so a lock excludes only other lock-takers and identify's phase-2 write has to defend itself. The predicate is `UPDATE faces SET person_id = ? WHERE id = ? AND person_id IS NULL AND embedding = ?`, and `id = ?` is what carries the deletion case: schema v8 made faces.id AUTOINCREMENT (R51), so a candidate a concurrent rebuild deleted in the phase-1-to-phase-2 gap takes its id out of circulation, and the write matches no row rather than landing on whichever face replaced it. Reproduced against the system libsqlite3 3.51.0 phig links: three candidates read as ids 21, 22 and 23 were deleted, their replacements were issued 24, 25 and 26, and the three writes labeled zero rows — with the embedding clause and without it. `person_id IS NULL` is the clause still doing live work: it makes this a compare-and-set against another labeler, which matters because two lock-free paths can reach the same candidate, and deleting it is the one edit to this predicate that fails IdentifyTest.AnUnchangedFaceIsStillLabeled. `embedding = ?` is belt-and-braces against a state phig cannot reach — R71. A losing write updates zero rows rather than throwing, which is why `labeled` counts changed rows and not statements issued.

### R49 — holds (test gap)

The advisory writer lock excludes only processes that construct one on the same file: no read takes it, and it never excludes a writer that takes none.

WriterLock is an flock(2) on a sidecar file, held for the object's lifetime and released by the kernel on process death, so there are no stale locks to clear. Advisory is the whole shape of the guarantee — every promise it makes is a promise about lock-takers, which is why the face subcommands and libphig's operations can run beside it by design rather than by accident. core/ constructs one only in acquire_catalog_lock, on the catalog's own lock file (R50). The CLI reaches that from nine branches of cli/main.cpp; the dry runs of rm, cp, mv and thumbs clean only read (R70) and take none. libphig constructs one only around its five metadata writes. models download takes a WriterLock on <models_dir>/.download.lock instead, a separate file that excludes only another download, since the models belong to no catalog. Measured with the built binary while a separate process held the flock on the catalog's phig.db.lock: search --count, duplicates, face list and tag list all completed normally, and so did a mutating 'phig face rebuild', while thumbs rebuild, rm and tag add were refused under --no-wait with 'Another phig operation is running'.

### R51 — holds

A face id names the same face for as long as that face exists: faces.id is AUTOINCREMENT, so a deleted id is never handed to a later insert.

A plain INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the rowid and is assigned max(rowid)+1, so deleting the highest face gives its id to the next insert — and a full face rebuild deletes and reinserts at the tail of this table for the whole collection, which makes that the steady state rather than a corner case. AUTOINCREMENT costs one sqlite_sequence row and buys the property the three lock-free face paths lean on. Schema v8 both creates the table that way and migrates an existing one by copying rows into faces_new with their ids preserved, deliberately leaving vec_faces untouched because it is keyed on faces.id and is a vec0 virtual table the copy cannot reach. Two comments in core/ still describe the pre-v8 world and are now wrong: core/faces_engine.h and core/database.h each say faces.id is 'INTEGER PRIMARY KEY without AUTOINCREMENT' and explain the surrounding defences as compensating for reuse that no longer happens. cli/main.cpp's cmd_face comment has the current version.

### R52 — holds (test gap)

A face rebuild reads an image's id inside the same transaction that writes that image's faces, so an image deleted while the worker waits for the write lock costs one skipped file rather than the whole run.

The gap between reading an id and opening the write transaction is two statements wide, and BEGIN IMMEDIATE waits on the 30-second busy timeout, so a concurrent rm holding the write lock holds that window open for as long as it likes. An insert against a deleted image_id violates the foreign key and throws, and parallel_for_each stops every worker on the first exception, so the cost of losing the race outside the transaction is the entire rebuild. Reading the id inside it means the write lock is already held and what was read cannot be deleted underneath it; a row that went before the transaction opened yields image_id < 0, a rollback and one recorded skip.

### R53 — holds (test gap)

The busy timeout is set before the connection issues its first statement, so a process opening a collection concurrently with another waits rather than failing.

PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL takes an exclusive lock to rewrite the file header, so the very first statement on a fresh connection is itself contendable. Setting sqlite3_busy_timeout after it leaves that one statement with no busy handler, which is what made DatabaseConcurrency.ConcurrentMigrationIsSafe flake at roughly one run in ten until 73d1e1a. The ordering is the whole rule: the same two calls in the other order compile, pass most runs, and fail under load.

### R54 — holds (test gap)

The connection is opened SQLITE_OPEN_FULLMUTEX explicitly, so one shared connection called from several threads is serialized by SQLite rather than by how the system SQLite was compiled.

libphig's header promises that a phig_ctx may be called concurrently from several threads, and a ctx holds one Database. A system SQLite compiled THREADSAFE=1 (serialized) mutexes every connection and the promise holds for free; one compiled THREADSAFE=2 (multi-thread) defaults to NOMUTEX, where sharing a connection is undefined and crashes rather than blocks. Asking for the flag means the ABI's promise does not depend on the packager's choice. That choice is not hypothetical and phig already ships against both: measured, Apple's system SQLite 3.51.0 — the library phig links on macOS, and the one the macOS CI leg builds against — reports sqlite3_threadsafe() == 2, and a connection opened there without the flag has a null sqlite3_db_mutex with no reconfiguration of any kind. So on macOS this flag is the only thing holding the header's promise up, and it is the ubuntu legs that would pass without it.

| Protects | db-row, user-metadata |

| Test gap | The two AbiMutate tests would also pass with the flag removed on a serialized build, because such a build mutexes the connection anyway. TheConnectionIsMutexedEvenWhereTheLibraryDefaultIsNot removes that dependence by putting the library in multi-thread mode for the length of the test — sqlite3_shutdown, sqlite3_config(SQLITE_CONFIG_MULTITHREAD), sqlite3_initialize, restored to the compile-time default on every exit — and asserting a control connection opened without the flag comes back with a null sqlite3_db_mutex before asking anything of phig's. Measured with the flag removed from Database::Database: sqlite3_db_mutex on the phig connection is null and the test fails. Two limits. The reconfiguration is process-global; it is safe under ctest, which runs each case as its own process, and was measured not to disturb a full in-order run of the whole suite in one process, but it is a hazard any new fixture holding a connection open across tests would create. And where the library refuses to be reconfigured the test skips rather than failing, so on such a build this rule is back to the two AbiMutate witnesses and the gap above. |

### R55 — holds

libphig's metadata writes take the writer lock without waiting and report PHIG_ERR_BUSY when it is held, and its long-running operations take no lock at all.

A GUI must not freeze behind a CLI job, so a contended lock is reported as an error the caller can surface rather than as a block — phig_acquire_write_lock passes no_wait = true, and PHIG_CATCH's LockBusy arm is the only path to PHIG_ERR_BUSY. The operations take none for a different reason: index's write set is unknowable before the walk, thumbs writes only the filesystem cache, and faces commits per image, so SQLite's own serialization is enough and small metadata writes stay serviceable for an operation's whole duration. A lock-holding operation would turn every tag write into PHIG_ERR_BUSY for the length of the run, which is the outcome this trade exists to avoid.

### R63 — holds

phig_last_error returns the calling thread's own last message, and only until that thread's next ABI call.

The storage is a function-local static thread_local std::string; PHIG_TRY clears it on entry and PHIG_CATCH sets it, so a later success on that thread wipes the message and a failure on another thread never appears in it. That is what lets a client drive one phig_ctx from several threads and still attribute an error to the call that produced it, which the handle-plus-poll operation model makes routine. The ctx argument is checked for null and otherwise ignored: the message is per-thread, not per-context, so two contexts used on one thread share the slot.

### R71 — holds (test gap)

A face row's embedding is written only by the insert that creates the row, so identify's `embedding = ?` clause refuses no write that `id = ?` and `person_id IS NULL` have not already refused.

Across core/, libphig/ and cli/ three statements update the faces table — `UPDATE faces SET image_id = ? WHERE image_id = ?` and the two that set person_id — and none of them writes embedding. The column is written by insert_face and by the v8 migration's `INSERT INTO faces_new (...) SELECT ... FROM faces`, both of which create rows rather than rewrite them. Re-detection is delete-and-reinsert — FacesEngine::run calls delete_faces_for_image then insert_face — which is also what keeps vec_faces in step, since it is keyed on faces.id, holds its own copy of the embedding, and is written only by those two functions. So the state this clause excludes, a row that keeps its id, stays unlabeled and carries a different embedding, is one phig cannot produce. The clause is kept deliberately: set_face_person_if_unchanged's header states it as the contract the caller wants, that the write refers to the face that was compared rather than to a row number, and as something that would catch an in-place embedding rewrite if one were added. Its cost is that phase 1 carries all 128 floats of every match into phase 2 to feed it, about 520 bytes per match where the id needs 8. Plan 044's work item 4 moves identify_person onto vec_faces KNN, which is where the choice lands: a KNN or paged phase 1 has to decide whether phase 2 still receives each matched embedding or only its id, and it cannot keep this clause without keeping the carry. 044 calls the transaction behaviour orthogonal to paging the read path, but that is about plan 031's phase split, not about this predicate's operands.

### R84 — holds

An image id names the same image for as long as that image exists: images.id is AUTOINCREMENT, so a deleted id is never handed to a later insert.

This is R51's property, for images instead of faces. Schema v9 declares images.id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT at core/database.cpp:539 and migrates an existing table by copying rows into images_new with their ids preserved, which seeds sqlite_sequence to the maximum so later inserts continue above it. Before v9 the column was a plain INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, which is the rowid and is assigned max(rowid)+1: measured against the system SQLite 3.51.0 phig links, three rows at ids 1-3 with the row at id 3 deleted gave id 3 to an unrelated path on the next insert. The ABI depends on this property — phig_query_page hands ids to a client and phig_tag_add, phig_gallery_set, phig_gallery_clear and phig_favorite_set take them back, with nothing between the read and the write to confirm the id still names the photo the caller saw — and reuse needed only a deletion at the tail of the table, which scan.reconcile and all four remove modes produce as ordinary operation. Plan 053's decision 2 makes an id the way every caller names a photo and 064 puts remove behind one, which is what raises the exposure from user-metadata to original-file. The migration could not reuse the v8 recipe: core/database.cpp:127 records that the faces rebuild is safe with foreign_keys=ON only because faces is a pure FK child, while image_tags.image_id and faces.image_id both reference images(id) ON DELETE CASCADE and the pragma is set on every open. SQLite's DROP TABLE deletes every row before dropping, so the rebuild would take every image_tags row and every faces row with it — measured, the tags and people tables survive intact but all tag and favorite assignments are gone and all face rows are gone, with their embeddings, boxes and person labels. No tag or person is destroyed; every association to one is. init_schema therefore runs every migration with foreign keys disabled rather than conditioning it on the version number, and apply_migration_step reads foreign_key_violations inside each step's transaction before and after the step, failing it before the commit on any violation the step added; violations already present are carried through (R88). That check does not cover the cascade case, which leaves no orphans and so adds no violation; ImagesMigrationV9.PreservesRowsIdsTagsFavoritesFacesAndLabels is what covers it, and it was confirmed to fail with the pragma re-enabled.

## cancellation

### R56 — holds (test gap)

Reconcile is not cancellable: run_reconcile takes no CancelToken, so a scan interrupted during its worker phase still relinks, demotes and deletes.

The phase mutates user-authored metadata inside one logged operation, and abandoning it halfway would leave the operation row stuck in_progress and the transfer passes half-applied — so it reads no token at all rather than reading one and ignoring it. That is why ScanEngine::run() is split: run_workers is cancellable, run_reconcile is not, and the split exists at exactly the boundary where a caller has to stop mapping a signal onto the token. cli/main.cpp destroys its ScopedInterruptHandler before calling run_reconcile so a Ctrl-C arriving during reconcile takes the default action instead of being silently swallowed. libphig never calls run_reconcile: the index operation is the additive half only.

### R57 — holds

Cancellation is polled only between whole items, so a run stopped by it leaves every item either fully done or untouched, and whatever committed before the stop stays committed.

parallel_for_each checks the token at the top of its work loop, before it claims the next index, so a worker never abandons an item it has started; scan, thumbs and faces inherit that by going through it. OrganizeEngine::apply has the same shape written by hand — the check is the first statement of its per-item loop, ahead of the destination re-check, execute_organize_action and carry_sidecars — so a cancellation cannot separate a media file from the attachment carried with it, even though a per-file error can (R48). Nothing is rolled back: rows and thumbnails already written stay, and the result reports cancelled = true and completed = false, which is what distinguishes a stopped run from a finished one. The claim is about cancellation alone and is deliberately narrower than 'an item is never half done' — R33 records the disk-then-log window that no token controls.

### R58 — partial (test gap)

A run whose token is already cancelled does no work and reports itself incomplete.

The four cancellable engines answer this differently. ThumbsEngine and FacesEngine each guard the empty-selection path on purpose — thumbs with 'images.empty() ? !cancel.stop() : parallel_for_each(...)' and faces with a token check placed ahead of its empty-selection return — because parallel_for_each returns true unconditionally for a zero-length range and would otherwise report an already-cancelled run over nothing as completed. ScanEngine and OrganizeEngine have no such guard: run_workers assigns result.completed only inside 'if (!files.empty())', so a cancelled scan of a directory holding no media files returns completed = true. apply sets result.cancelled inside its per-item loop and derives completed after the loop from !cancelled and the error counts; a loop that never runs sees no cancel, so a cancelled apply of an empty plan returns cancelled = false and completed = true. Through the ABI that is the difference between PHIG_OP_DONE and PHIG_OP_CANCELLED: the scan wrapper derives the terminal state from completed, and organize's wrapper returns !cancelled. Read from the code and corroborated by the test asymmetry — thumbs and faces each have an empty-selection case, scan and organize have none — not measured, because nothing outside the engines can produce an already-cancelled run over an empty selection on demand. The claim is provisional: 056 is the open plan that owns what an operation reports about its own status, and it does not name this.

### R67 — holds

phig_op_free joins the operation's worker rather than detaching it, so no engine thread outlives the handle or the Database it writes through.

The worker holds raw pointers to the phig_op and to the per-operation Database the handle owns, so returning while it still runs would leave it writing through freed memory — a use-after-free onto a live SQLite connection, which is the shape of corruption a client can neither see nor recover from. Joining makes phig_op_free block for as long as the item in flight takes; a caller that does not want to wait calls phig_op_cancel first, and cancellation lands between items (R57), so the wait is bounded by one item rather than by the run. phig_op_wait is the same join without the free.

### R61 — violated (test gap)

A destructive operation's preview is a value the caller can inspect, not text the engine prints.

OrganizeEngine::plan returns an OrganizePlan — one entry per file carrying source, intended destination, resolved destination, whether it conflicts, and whether phig tracks the occupant — which is why cp and mv have a dry run on every surface and libphig can expose phig_organize_plan_source_at and its siblings. Remove has the opposite shape: cmd_rm computes the same information and writes it to std::cout as prose, including the [DRY RUN] listing at remove_exec.cpp:129-130 and the skip counts above it, and returns an int. A caller that is not a terminal gets nothing — no list, no counts, no way to render 'these 412 files will be deleted' — so remove cannot take the plan/apply shape R66 requires until its preview becomes data. This is the load-bearing half of a wider drift from core/CLAUDE.md, which says an engine carries no user-facing prose and that wording is the caller's job: 23 lines across seven core/ files write to std::cout, std::cerr or stderr — remove_exec.cpp (10), models.cpp (8), config.cpp:138, hasher.cpp:309, lockfile.cpp:59, log.cpp:97 and organize_exec.cpp:134. The other thirteen are diagnostics and progress cosmetics; these ten are an operation's result. log.cpp:97 is counted although it is the logger's own open failure rather than an operation's output: it is the one write with no alternative, since the mechanism that would otherwise carry the message is the thing that failed.

### R66 — partial (test gap)

A destructive ABI operation is authorized by a plan the caller inspects and then applies with a second call, never by a callback the engine invokes mid-run.

No ABI entry point takes a confirmation callback and none can: no callback may run on an engine thread under the handle-plus-poll model, and a callback has no meaning over the wire protocol plan 052 designs, where nothing can call back into a browser mid-request. cmd_rm's ConfirmFn is a cli/ affordance for a command with no plan phase, not a model to copy. Organize is the worked example and carries all three properties the shape is meant to bring: the plan is a caller-owned value that phig_op_organize_plan_take copies out and the caller frees, so it outlives the operation that computed it and start_apply snapshots it again on the way in; apply re-verifies every decision at execution time, so a stale plan cannot cause an action the re-check would not independently justify; and which decisions are overridable is a property of the decision type rather than of the mechanism (R59). The gap is faces: phig_op_faces_start is destructive — operations.toml marks faces.rebuild so, and R60 measures what it destroys — and it has no plan phase, so the one ABI operation that deletes user-authored metadata is the one with no authorization step. Remove and reconcile are not counterexamples: neither is reachable through the ABI yet, which 053 and 041 own.

### R68 — violated (test gap)

Trash empty destroys its contents permanently and only after authorization: an empty trash returns without asking, --yes skips the prompt, and otherwise it refuses outright unless run at an interactive terminal where the operator types the literal string 'yes' in response to a prompt naming the item count and the trash directory.

Trash is what makes rm's default mode recoverable (R23): the row goes, the bytes stay in <catalog>/trash. cmd_trash_empty in cli/main.cpp is where that recoverability ends — it is the one command with no restore snapshot and no activity-log entry behind it, so whatever it deletes is gone. The guard guarding that step is real, and it is the same shape as R22's hard-delete guard: it short-circuits on an empty trash before asking anything, otherwise prints the count and directory, refuses non-interactively so a piped 'yes' cannot bypass it, and only proceeds once the operator types 'yes' at a TTY; --yes exists for a caller that has already decided. What it deletes is every entry in <catalog>/trash, and a catalog can be any directory the user names, so `phig --catalog ~/Pictures scan ...` makes ~/Pictures/trash phig's trash, including a trash/ that was there before; nothing checks that phig put an entry there before removing it, and plan 064 owns that check. But the guard is cli/main.cpp code with no core/ counterpart: operations.toml's own trash.empty entry names cli/main.cpp:cmd_trash_empty as its core_entry, remarking that no core/ primitive exists for it. So libphig has nothing to call, a future phigd has nothing to call, and the GTK client has nothing to call — each would have to reimplement the confirmation rather than inherit it, which is exactly the failure mode root CLAUDE.md's 'enforcement belongs in core/ or libphig/, never cli/' rule exists to name. libphig/CLAUDE.md already lists 'Remove — rm's modes, trash empty' as missing ABI coverage under 053, and libphig links phig-core rather than cli/, so 053 cannot expose trash.empty without moving this guard into core/ first. Anchored at cli/main.cpp deliberately: the location is the defect, and status is violated for exactly that reason rather than because the guard is wrong.

### R70 — holds (test gap)

A command that only reads a collection neither creates its database nor migrates its schema.

open_catalog_db is the one open policy. Read opens read-only, so it can neither create the file nor migrate it, and it refuses a missing database and any schema version other than this build's with a CatalogError naming the catalog. Write and Create migrate; only Create makes a missing database. So of the commands that write, only scan and libphig's read-write context create a missing catalog; every other write opens with Write, or calls require_catalog before taking its lock, and refuses a missing catalog without creating its directory. Which access a command passes is decided at its call site: every CLI command that only reads, including the dry runs of rm, cp, mv and thumbs clean, passes Read. libphig's read-only context passes Read too, through open_catalog_db, so it refuses a missing database or another schema version the same way. A migration is forward-only and init_schema refuses a database newer than the build, so a read that migrated would make the catalog unopenable by an older phig on another machine. A read that created would turn a mistyped catalog path into an empty catalog reported as empty. The refusal of a newer catalog also covers a concurrent upgrade: another build can upgrade past this one between open_catalog_db's read and init_schema's transactions, a window the pre-upgrade copy widens, and every step and schema path then finds its version already reached and skips. init_schema therefore re-reads the version where every path ends and throws SchemaNewerError, which open_catalog_db turns into the same CatalogError::Kind::Newer it raises for its own read, so the open does not succeed against a schema this build does not know. It does not stop another build upgrading the catalog later, while this connection stays open.

### R73 — holds (test gap)

Input an operation does not recognize, whether an unknown CLI flag or an option value outside its field's defined set, stops it before it changes anything.

An unrecognized input that is skipped or defaulted widens what an operation acts on without anyone asking for it. The CLI case was measured: before face rebuild's flag loop had an else branch, `phig face rebuild --mtach '*a.jpg'` stepped over the typo and its value, left opts.matches empty, which selects every image (R74), and rebuilt both images of a two-image collection, dropping the label on a named face; with the else branch the same typo prints 'Unknown option: --mtach', exits 1, and the face row and its label are untouched. All thirteen of cli/main.cpp's flag loops now end that way. That guard is argv parsing, which only cli/ has, so the rule is enforced again below it for every surface: each engine's validate() throws InvalidOption before any work for a value outside its field's set (scan's media string and directory, a thumbnail size of zero or less, organize's empty destination or format, and a parallel above 256, or above the machine's core count where each worker loads its own ~150MB face detector), and libphig refuses an enum value outside its declaration (phig_config.mode, phig_index_options.media, on_conflict, a per-item resolution), a negative thumbnail size, and an id_count with a NULL ids array, returning PHIG_ERR_INVALID_ARG with *out NULL and the field named in phig_last_error. Before that, each of those was defaulted: an unknown mode opened the read-write path, which creates a missing catalog; an unknown media indexed everything; an unknown conflict policy became rename; an empty destination planned every path relative to the process's working directory.

### R74 — holds (test gap)

An operation acts on every tracked path that no --exclude matches and, when any --match was given, that at least one --match matches; with no --match at all it acts on everything.

One function decides this for every command: passes_selection checks the excludes first and returns false on the first hit, so exclude wins wherever the two overlap and an excluded path cannot be moved, deleted, re-detected or relabelled by the run that excluded it. The second half is the one that surprises. With an empty match list the function returns true for every path, so `phig rm --exclude '*.png'` selects the whole collection minus the PNGs rather than nothing, and `phig face rebuild` with no flags selects every image. Both are deliberate and both have a guard elsewhere rather than here: rm's broad-selection confirmation covers the first (R22), and tag, gallery and fav refuse an unnamed selection outright (R78). The comparison is against the whole path, not the basename — callers pass img.path — so an exclude may name a directory. Seven call sites in all: five in core/ (faces_engine.cpp:81, organize_engine.cpp:76, remove_exec.cpp:82, thumbs_engine.cpp:28, search_engine.cpp:100) and two in cli/ (main.cpp:489 and :1538, the second being select_paths, which is how tag, gallery and fav reach it).

### R77 — violated (test gap)

Cleaning the thumbnail cache removes only files whose names match phig's thumbnail contract and whose hash no row claims, and a dry run removes nothing at all.

The cache directory is not phig's private space: thumbnails live in <catalog>/thumbs, resolved by current_catalog(), and a catalog can be any directory, so a recursive delete over it could take files phig never wrote. It cleans only its own catalog's thumbs/: another catalog's cache, even one holding the same orphaned name, is never visited. Every regular file under it is tested with is_thumbnail_filename — a 64-hex stem and a .jpg suffix — and anything else is counted as foreign and left, then a thumbnail whose stem is in db.get_all_sha256s() is kept and the rest are removed. --dry-run prints the same list and removes nothing, including the sweep of emptied subdirectories, which is skipped as a whole rather than per entry. Measured with the built binary against a scratch thumbnail directory holding one orphaned thumbnail and one notes.txt: `thumbs clean --dry-run` printed 'Would remove 1 orphaned thumbnails' and 'Left untouched 1 non-thumbnail files in the cache directory' and left both files where they were; the same command without the flag removed the thumbnail and left notes.txt with its bytes intact. Recorded as violated for where the guard lives, not for what it does. is_thumbnail_filename is a core/ predicate, but the loop that consults it, the dry-run branch and the directory sweep are all in cli/main.cpp, and no core/ primitive cleans a thumbnail cache — libphig/CLAUDE.md lists `thumbs clean` among what the ABI cannot reach, noting that the loop itself is in cli/, and 053 owns closing that. A client that grew its own cache cleaning would inherit none of this.

### R78 — holds

A metadata write refuses to run unless the caller named which images it applies to.

tag add, tag remove, gallery set, gallery clear, fav add and fav remove each require at least one --match or a --path and exit 1 otherwise. Without that check the selection resolves to every row in the collection, since an empty filter matches everything (R74): `phig tag remove holiday` would strip that tag collection-wide and `phig gallery clear` would empty every gallery, both silently, both destroying user-authored metadata nothing can rebuild, and neither leaving a trace — metadata.write opens no logged operation, so there is no restore snapshot and no activity-log entry to read afterwards. The refusal is resolve_named_selection in core/selection.cpp, which returns nullopt when the caller named nothing at all; naming a selection that happens to match nothing is a different thing and returns an empty list, because the caller said what it wanted and nothing qualified. It sits on the resolve step rather than on the write because the write cannot see the hazard: set_tag_by_ids and set_gallery_by_ids receive an id list and cannot tell a caller that asked for the whole collection from one that forgot to filter. Resolution is where the omission is still visible, and putting it there is what makes it inheritable — a future phigd accepting a glob over HTTP calls the same function and gets the same refusal rather than reimplementing the check, which a cli/-only guard could not offer. The ABI needs none of it: phig_tag_add and its five neighbours take an explicit array of ids, so a client cannot ask for everything by omission. Plan 053 step 5 moved the guard here from three copies in cli/main.cpp, which is why this was recorded violated for its location; cli/ now renders the nullopt as its error and supplies only the wording.

### R87 — holds (test gap)

Every destination organize plans lies inside the destination directory the caller named; nothing a file carries and nothing in the format can place a file outside it.

A format's tokens are substituted into a path joined onto the destination, and %camera, %make and %gallery come from the file's EXIF Model and Make and its gallery name, which a camera writes and anyone can edit. Substituted verbatim, a '/' adds directories, a '..' climbs out and an absolute value replaces the destination; measured with the built binary, a JPEG whose Model was '../../escaped' was copied two directories above the destination, and one whose Make was '/tmp/abs' was planned into /tmp/abs. The caller authorized a move into one directory, not wherever the file says, so three guards hold the line. apply_format expands each of those tokens to a single path component: '/' and '\' become '_', control characters are dropped, and a value left empty, '.' or '..' takes its placeholder. validate(const OrganizeOptions&) refuses, before planning, a format that is an absolute path, has a '..' component, or uses an unknown token, which also catches a typo such as %y that would otherwise name a folder. OrganizeEngine::plan then checks each built destination lexically lies under the destination and throws if one does not; after the other two that cannot happen, so reaching it is a bug and no plan is produced. The R01 and R02 conflict guards are separate: they stop an overwrite at a path, these stop the path being outside the tree.
